name: Normal vs. fat-tailed distributions
originator: Vilfredo Pareto (1896); Benoît Mandelbrot (1963); Nassim Taleb (2007)
rule: Heights cluster near an average. Wealth, city sizes, earthquakes and book sales follow power laws, where averages mislead and rare extremes dominate.
plain: In some worlds the biggest event is only a bit bigger than the average. In others, one event can be bigger than all the rest combined.
formula: Normal: P(x) ∝ e^(−x²/2σ²)   ·   Power law: P(X > x) ∝ x^(−α)

story.beat: The hull has taken 500 micrometeoroid hits in 10 years, all tiny, and the average hit is harmless. Rook wants to cut shielding. You plot the hit sizes: a power law. The rare big impact isn't a bit worse than average; it could be thousands of times worse. The shield budget stays.

examples.text: Two traders out of 200 hold most of the colony's credits. The 'average wealth' describes nobody.
Colonists' heights are normal: nobody is 5 metres tall. Their follower counts on the colony net are fat-tailed.
Most solar flares are harmless; the rare giant one can fry every circuit, so plan for the tail.

realCase.title: Long-Term Capital Management
realCase.text: A hedge fund run by star traders and two Nobel-winning economists used models that treated extreme market moves as near-impossible. Heavily borrowed, it lost about $4.6 billion in a few months after Russia's debt default, and the New York Fed organised a bank-funded rescue to prevent wider damage.

misuse: Treating '80/20' as a law of nature, or calling everything a 'black swan' after the fact to excuse bad planning.
sources: Mark Newman, 'Power laws, Pareto distributions and Zipf's law', Contemporary Physics (2005)

predict.prompt: 500 small hull hits so far. Impact sizes follow a power law. The worst future hit is likely…
options: possibly far larger than anything seen so far
predict.why: Fat tails mean the past maximum isn't a ceiling.

mcq.why: City sizes follow a power law.

whichModel.prompt: A publisher's one bestseller outsells its other 500 books combined.
